title: Tribal Trustees
summary: Shinnecock tribal trusteeship began under New York law in 1792, shaping community governance and lease records in the 1790s.
content:
Introduction

In 1792, Shinnecock's Tribal Trustee system was established by the State of New York when the three-person (male) trustee system of tribal government went into effect.1

History

1793

The 'Receipt for Indian Lease' for Shinnecock's 1703 lease of the Shinnecock Hills was signed on April 13, 1793, by Absalom Cuffee, David Jacobs, and Abraham Jacobs of the Shinnecock Nation.

This major agreement also established the Shinnecock Trustee system which is still in effect today. The townspeople wanted to establish a convenient system for leasing Shinnecock lands to white farmers. It was an important first step toward seizing the hills, but ironically, it also created a very effective system of governance for the Shinnecock which has enabled them to preserve our heritage and assist with protecting ancient lands.2

1816

A meeting of the Magistrates (of the town of Southampton & Shinnecock Indian Nation trustees April 8th, 1816.3

Voted that there be one hundred acres laid out in Shinnecock
Voted that the trustees repair the fence & clear the Neck.
Voted that no one shall have a garden laid out except where he lives.

David Rose, Wm Herrick, James Peirson - Southampton Justices

Ab Jacob, David Walkus, James Waberton - Shinnecock Trustees

1992

In 1992 the Shinnecock Nation extended to resident female tribal members the right to elect tribal Trustees and vote on tribal business.4

In that same year, the Shinnecock established a thirteen-member Tribal Council, elected for two-year terms, to serve as an advisory body and communications facilitation group within the Nation.4

2013

In February 2013, the Shinnecock Nation passed a constitution that overhauled their entire government. The three-member Trustee board was phased out and on December 10th, 2014, replaced by a seven-member Council of Trustees. The Council is the traditional way of governing before the State of NY imposing the three-man Trustee system on the Shinnecock Nation in 1792.5

1934 land-leasing initiative

Hunter described a 1934 initiative in which the Trustee Board appointed a committee to present reservation residents with a proposal for leasing unused land. She associated Harry B. Thompson, Elliott A. Kellis, Oliver Kellis, Frederick Arch, Eugene Cuffee, Charles S. Bunn, and Seymour Eleazer with the effort. In Hunter's 1950 account, rent from land leased to non-Native farmers was divided among reservation families and the leases also created some agricultural work. This is Hunter's historical description of the trustee system and should not be read as a description of current Shinnecock governance or land policy.1

An appointed woman clerk, 1934–1940

Hunter wrote that Shinnecock was without a clerk in 1934 and that the trustees appointed an unnamed woman who served through 1940. She called this the first time since Quashawan that a woman had a voice in “strict tribal matters.” The passage documents an appointed clerk and record-keeping role; it should not be confused with election as chair or trustee, and Hunter did not supply the clerk’s name.1

Questions visitors ask

Open a question for a concise answer, context, and sources.

How have Native forms of leadership and tribal government changed over time?

Long Island records preserve councils, sachems, sunksquaws, elders, and kin-based leadership. Colonial and state systems later pressed communities into trustee structures, while Native people continued to adapt those institutions and contest exclusions from political participation.

Surviving records describe several forms of leadership rather than one unchanged system. Sachems, sunksquaws, elders, families, and councils appear in diplomacy, land negotiations, and community decision-making. Colonial officials often preferred a single signer whose authority could be made legible to European law, and New York later formalized trustee systems. Those systems narrowed or altered older forms of authority and, at times, excluded women. Shinnecock women's efforts to regain voting participation culminated in the April 4, 1994 trustee election, connecting a modern election with a much longer record of Indigenous women's leadership.
